## The A.I. Fight Dividing the Trump Administration, and the Next James Bond


#### Plus, a new study on phone bans in schools.


2026-11-17T06:00:07-05:00


This transcript was created using speech recognition software. While it has been reviewed by human transcribers, it may contain errors. Please review the episode audio before quoting from this transcript and email transcripts@nytimes.com with any questions.


tracy mumford


From “The New York Times,” it’s “The Headlines.” I’m Tracy Mumford. Today’s Tuesday, November 17. Here’s what we’re covering.


\[LIGHT MUSIC\]


A divide within the Trump administration over technology and China has broken into the open right as President Trump is headed to meet with Xi Jinping. On one side is Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary whose department writes and enforces the rules around exporting AI chips. Lutnick has taken a soft touch on that.


commerce secretary howard lutnick


You want to sell the Chinese enough that their developers get addicted to the American technology stack.


tracy mumford


On the other side is a group of top administration officials who’ve been pressing for months for stricter limits on what chips China can access.


treasury secretary scott bessent


Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies, and the AI race gives the Chinese an advantage.


tracy mumford


That group includes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security advisor, and much of the National Security Council staff. And now that tough on China side seems to be gaining traction.


Yesterday the administration moved to crack down on a loophole that has allowed China to access offshore data centers, basically renting the kind of advanced chips it’s not allowed to buy directly. And late last night, the justice and commerce departments announced they’re pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a company suspected of chip smuggling whose former executive had an affair with Jensen Huang of NVIDIA. For its part, Megaspeed says it’s complied with all laws. The investigation announcement appeared to be a response to criticism that the case under Lutnick’s leadership had moved too slowly.


\[LIGHT MUSIC\]


Yesterday, on the heels of the FAA’s ground stop and the Microsoft outage, two other institutions hit technical issues, United Airlines and Chase Bank. United said it had a “widespread system outage” that lasted for about an hour in the afternoon, leading to delays. The airline hasn’t provided additional details about the cause of the outage, which comes just as millions of Americans are preparing to fly for the week of Thanksgiving.


And for JPMorgan Chase, the nation’s largest bank, some customers reported on social media yesterday that they couldn’t use their ATM cards or complete transactions at branches. Chase says it’s now resumed normal operations after experiencing, quote, “a temporary issue related to a software bug.” It said there was no evidence that the problem was cyber related. With the back-to-back-to-back incidents, one professor of information technology at Notre Dame said each example has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but that they all underscore, quote, “the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day.”


\[LIGHT MUSIC\]


Across the country over the past few years —


indiana news


Indiana State law now requires schools to make their students leave their phones at home.


tracy mumford


— dozens of states have banned or restricted cell phone use in schools.


new jersey news


Following in New York’s footsteps, students in New Jersey will not have access to those cell phones during the school day.


tracy mumford


Now, a large new study has found that those policies are starting to gradually improve test scores. The analysis, published by Harvard Center for Education Policy Research, looked at test scores for more than 3 million elementary through high school students over five years, and it compared kids scores in schools that put in place strict phone bans to those at schools without them.


The biggest improvements were in schools with the strictest bans, like ones that require students to lock their phones in pouches the whole day. There, scores improved as much as if students had an extra week or two of school a year. There have been studies on this topic before with mixed results, but this new study is the first to track individual students’ performance before and after bans were put in place.


One education researcher who was not involved in the study cautioned against being too optimistic about modest achievement gains but said that if they continue to add up over time year after year, it could be, quote, “really important and really meaningful.” Teachers and researchers also say that improving test scores is just one potential benefit of phone bans, which can also cut back on cyberbullying, get kids more engaged in the classroom, and boost social skills.


\[LIGHT MUSIC\]


Earlier this fall, my colleague Hiroko Tabuchi went on a reporting trip to Arizona to check out what’s known as an aircraft boneyard.


hiroko tabuchi


It’s in the middle of the Sonoran Desert, and there are hundreds of planes that are parked basically nose to tail. The airplanes were in various states of disrepair. You could even peek in to see seats, even tray tables and remnants of meals and things like that. They’re all waiting there to be stripped for parts.


And one of the parts that’s gained a lot of attention recently are their powerful jet engines. These jet engines from these old aircraft are now being used for something surprising. They’re being used to generate power for data centers.


tracy mumford


Hiroko says what’s happening is that in the rush to power the data center boom across the US, companies are getting creative about how to generate as much electricity as quickly as possible. And old jet engines are a plentiful and untapped source that doesn’t rely on the grid. The engines can be pulled off the wings of planes and converted into generators.


But it’s raising alarms with environmentalists. They say that repurposed aircraft turbines tend to be less efficient and more polluting than the kinds of engines that are specifically designed for gas-burning burning power plants. So far, Elon Musk’s AI company xAI has installed eight converted turbines in Mississippi to power one of its massive data centers, according to state permits and satellite imagery. And other state permits show that more big AI companies also have plans to use turbines from a company that repurposes jet engines.


Meanwhile, a major new study has given the clearest picture yet of how the data center boom has sent carbon emissions soaring. The research, published yesterday in the journal “Nature Sustainability,” found that the largest data centers in the US are responsible for releasing almost as much carbon dioxide a year as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark, and that’s likely to be a significant undercount, since the study only went through the first half of last year. And since then, according to one estimate, at least 250 more data centers have come online.


\[LIGHT MUSIC\]


And finally —


speaker 1


Who are you?


sean connery as james bond


Bond, James Bond.


tracy mumford


Sean Connery kicked things off.


roger moore as james bond


Any man who drinks Dom Perignon ‘52 can’t be all bad.


tracy mumford


Roger Moore brought the camp.


pierce brosnan as james bond


Vodka martini, shaken, not stirred.


tracy mumford


Pierce Brosnan made him suave.


daniel craig as james bond


Some men are coming to kill us. We’re going to kill them first.


tracy mumford


Daniel Craig came in and made him a bruiser. Now we’re getting our first millennial James Bond. It’s Robert Pattinson, your favorite sparkly teenage vampire.


alissa wilkinson


A lot of people first knew Robert Pattinson from his role in “Twilight.” But in the years after that, he’s worked with tons of great auteur directors, and he often plays very weird, almost pathetic guys, people who are down on their luck or who are getting beaten up on. Or maybe they’re very craven and cowardly, as in this summer’s role in “The Odyssey.” So it’s not the kind of character that you would necessarily expect the new James Bond to be playing. But I think that that actually is one of the things that makes him great for the role.


tracy mumford


Alissa Wilkinson is a film critic at “The Times.” She says people are having a lot of feelings about the casting, which was announced yesterday. Some think Pattinson s too weird. Or they love that he’s weird, and they worry that this will cut him off from more interesting roles.


It is a good time to be reminded that Daniel Craig was not everybody’s favorite choice back in the day. Some people called him a potato — harsh — and even created a protest website, craignotbond.com.


Looking ahead, we’re not likely to see Pattinson’s 007 for a while, 2028 at the very earliest. The last film came out in 2021. So that would be the longest we’ve ever gone without a Bond movie since the franchise debuted.


\[THEME MUSIC\]


Those are “The Headlines.” Today on “The Daily,” what Democrats in Congress will and won’t be able to do about the country’s affordability crisis when they take power in January. You can find that in “The New York Times” app or wherever you get your podcasts. I’m Tracy Mumford. We’ll be back tomorrow.


\[THEME MUSIC\]


Nov. 17, 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET
